g-pos-06.reason: 'made it ___ easier' needs an adverb modifying the comparative 'easier'; only 'dramatically' fits. 'dramatic' cannot premodify a comparative adjective.
g-pos-06.why: Standard Part 5 word-form item with a long business stem; the comparative-modifier slot is a real ETS pattern.
g-pos-06.editorNote: 'front desk' also appears in g-pos-07, v-family-07 and l-talk-01; vary the setting.

g-tense-02.reason: 'Currently' + an ongoing single action ('this morning's outage') requires present progressive. Simple present 'investigate' would express habit and is unidiomatic here; past/present perfect clash with 'currently' and 'may load slowly until early afternoon'.
g-tense-02.why: The signal word 'Currently' is at the head of the sentence and the whole second clause confirms it; real items usually bury the time cue.
g-tense-02.fix: Move the cue later or use a subtler one (e.g. 'still', 'at the moment') to make the item medium.

g-connect-03.reason: Sentence-initial conjunctive adverb followed by a comma; the second sentence contrasts with the first, so 'However'. 'Therefore' reverses the logic; 'Whereas' is a subordinator and cannot introduce a free-standing sentence with a comma; 'In spite of' needs a noun phrase.
g-connect-03.why: Classic connector item with one adverb, one subordinator and one preposition as distractors, exactly the ETS distribution.

g-participle-01.reason: Attributive past participle 'updated price list' (the list has been updated). 'updating' would mean the list is doing the updating; 'update(s)' as a noun compound is not idiomatic.
g-participle-01.why: Very short stem, no business context, and 'updated price list' is an extremely common collocation; slightly below typical ETS length and difficulty.
g-participle-01.fix: Lengthen the stem (e.g. a clause about what changed) and consider 'revised' vs 'revising' style options for a bit more resistance.

g-pos-07.reason: The gap modifies the verb phrase 'find the Pembry Conference Center', so an adverb is needed: 'easily'. 'easy' as flat adverb is informal and not accepted in formal writing.
g-pos-07.why: Long, realistic stem; the position after a direct object is a legitimate adverb-slot test.

g-pos-08.reason: Main verb needed for the subject 'The results'; plural subject agrees with 'indicate'. Other forms are noun/adjective/participle and leave the sentence without a finite verb.
g-pos-08.why: Standard 'find the missing finite verb' item; the intervening 'of last month's customer survey' is the one small trap for agreement.

g-tense-06.reason: 'for thirty-two years when she retires at the end of next month' anchors the duration to a future point, so future perfect 'will have been'. Present perfect would need 'so far'/'now'; 'had been' needs a past reference point.
g-tense-06.why: Future perfect with a present-tense time clause is a genuine ETS pattern, and the long non-restrictive relative clause is the kind of noise real stems contain.
g-tense-06.editorNote: 'straight out of university' reads slightly British; 'straight out of college' is more typical of ETS American register.

g-connect-06.reason: The warehouse WILL accept late deliveries only under a condition, so 'provided that'. 'unless' and 'even if' invert the logic; 'so that' would make the driver's arrangement a purpose, which is impossible with a completed action ('has arranged ... in advance').
g-connect-06.why: Good conditional-connector item with a plausible 'unless' lure.
g-connect-06.editorNote: The logic is slightly odd: staffed until 5 p.m. but the exception starts 'after 6 p.m.'. Either say 'after 5 p.m.' or reframe ('will not accept deliveries after 5 p.m. unless...').

g-participle-05.reason: Reduced passive relative clause: 'The consultants (who were) hired last spring ... have recommended'. 'were hired' would give the sentence two finite verbs with no conjunction; 'hiring' would make the consultants the ones doing the hiring.
g-participle-05.why: Textbook ETS trap: the finite verb 'have recommended' is far from the gap, so 'were hired' looks tempting.

g-prep-05.reason: 'stored in accordance with the guidelines' is the only phrase that makes sense with rules/guidelines. 'in response to' and 'in addition to' are semantically wrong; 'on behalf of' takes a person/organisation.
g-prep-05.why: Multi-word preposition item with a suitably long stem.
g-prep-05.editorNote: 'on behalf of' here is the answer to g-prep-07 in the same set. Replace it with something like 'in exchange for' or 'by means of' so one item does not eliminate an option in another.

g-prep-06.reason: 'attribute X to Y' is a fixed pattern; the direct object ('most of the drop in second-quarter shipments') is long, which is the intended trap. No other preposition collocates with 'attribute'.
g-prep-06.why: Verb + dependent preposition with a long object separating verb and gap; very ETS-like.

g-prep-07.reason: 'I am writing on behalf of [organisation] to invite you' is the standard opening formula. 'in favor of'/'in charge of'/'in case of' produce nonsense.
g-prep-07.why: The phrase is one of the most frequent formulas in TOEIC letters, and the three distractors are far from the target meaning, so almost every candidate above beginner level gets it.
g-prep-07.fix: Use a closer distractor pair (e.g. 'on account of', 'in place of') or move the gap to a less formulaic slot.

g-voice-02.reason: 'Shipping costs' rise by themselves, so the intransitive 'rise' is needed; 'raise' (A, D) requires an object. 'since the start of the year' requires a perfect form, ruling out 'are rising'.
g-voice-02.why: rise/raise plus a perfect-tense cue is a real ETS pairing; a fourth option such as 'have been rising' would have been an even better near-miss than 'have been raising'.

g-toing-01.reason: 'decide' takes a to-infinitive: 'has decided to postpone'. The other forms do not complement 'decide'.
g-toing-01.why: Short stem and a basic verb-pattern; below the usual ETS difficulty for this category.
g-toing-01.fix: Use a verb whose complement is less universally known (e.g. 'agreed', 'arranged', 'put off' vs 'postpone' + gerund) or add more stem context.

g-relative-04.reason: 'it believes' is a parenthetical; the relative pronoun is the subject of 'are best qualified', so 'who'. 'whom' is the classic hypercorrection lure; 'which' cannot refer to people in a defining clause; 'whose' needs a following noun.
g-relative-04.why: This is exactly the who/whom-with-parenthetical trap that appears in genuine ETS items; the plural verb 'are' gives an attentive reader the clue.
g-relative-04.editorNote: Usage note only: MWDEU records 'whom' as common in this frame, but every major style guide (Chicago, AP, Garner) treats 'who' as correct in formal writing, so the key stands.

g-agree-04.reason: 'Each of the [plural]' takes a singular verb; the intervening 'including the three that opened in Asia' is the plural lure. 'have required' would not produce the required passive; 'being' leaves no finite verb.
g-agree-04.why: 'Each of ... is' with a long plural interrupter is one of the most reliable ETS agreement items.

g-quantity-04.reason: 'errors' is a count noun, so 'fewer' in formal writing; 'less' is the informal lure. 'fewest'/'little' do not fit 'than'.
g-quantity-04.why: The less/fewer distinction is well known to TOEIC candidates; the long stem does not add much resistance. Solid but easy.
g-quantity-04.editorNote: Descriptive authorities (MWDEU) accept 'less' with count nouns in informal use, but formal business writing and every ETS key use 'fewer'; no ambiguity for the test.

g-mandative-03.reason: 'recommended that the team ___' is a mandative that-clause; American formal English uses the base form (present subjunctive) 'check'. 'checks' is the -s lure; 'checked'/'is checking' are not used in mandative clauses.
g-mandative-03.why: Subjunctive after 'recommend' with a distant verb and a long stem is a genuine ETS hard item.
g-mandative-03.editorNote: Flag, not ambiguity: British formal usage (Quirk et al., Cambridge Grammar) accepts the indicative 'checks' in mandative clauses. TOEIC keys follow American practice, so D is the only defensible key; keep the item but be aware a British-trained candidate may dispute it.

g-compare-04.reason: 'twice as [adjective] as' is the only multiplier comparison pattern; 'so ... as' is used only in negatives, 'more ... as' and 'much ... as' are ungrammatical.
g-compare-04.why: Multiplier + equative is a recurring ETS pattern; 'so' is a fair lure.

g-toing-04.reason: 'contribute to' takes a noun or gerund: 'contributed significantly to reducing the time'. 'to reduce' is the infinitive lure; 'reducing' alone and 'for reducing' lack the required preposition.
g-toing-04.why: Preposition-'to' + gerund (contribute/look forward/object/committed to) is a classic ETS trap, and the adverb between verb and gap makes it harder.

g-pronoun-04.reason: The verb is plural ('are entitled'), so the subject must be plural: 'Those who registered'. 'Anyone'/'Whoever' would require 'is'; 'Them' cannot be a subject.
g-pronoun-04.why: The plural verb is the only disambiguator, sitting a full clause away from the gap; that is a proper ETS-style trap.

g-conditional-03.reason: Inverted conditional 'Should you have any questions, please...' is the standard formal formula. 'Had you have' is ungrammatical; 'Would you have' would be a question; 'Unless you have any questions, please contact' is illogical.
g-conditional-03.why: Common ETS formula; 'Unless' is the meaning trap and 'Had' the form trap.

v-collocation-07.reason: 'fall short of (a target)' is the fixed idiom. 'run short of' means to have insufficient supply of something and does not take 'a target'; 'cut short' and 'draw' do not fit.
v-collocation-07.why: 'ran' is a genuinely tempting near-miss; this is the kind of collocation item ETS writes.

v-collocation-08.reason: 'lodge a complaint' is the collocation; 'house', 'host' and 'board' are all accommodation verbs chosen as semantic decoys but none takes 'complaint'.
v-collocation-08.why: Good lexical item; distractors are thematically linked (lodging/hosting), which is a real ETS technique.

v-collocation-09.reason: 'bear in mind' (also 'keep in mind', not offered). 'take/put/carry in mind' are not idiomatic.
v-collocation-09.why: Very common phrase in TOEIC notices; 'take' is the only plausible lure.
v-collocation-09.editorNote: Stem topic (parking garage closed on Saturday) overlaps with l-qr-10; different sections, no answer leak, but vary if convenient.

v-synonym-02.reason: The department gives equipment temporarily and the users are 'borrowers' who 'must return' it, so 'lends'. 'borrows' reverses the direction; 'donates' contradicts 'return'; 'rents' implies payment, which is not implied for an internal IT department.
v-synonym-02.why: lend/borrow reversal is a standard TOEIC item; 'rents' is the only other option a careless reader could keep.
v-synonym-02.editorNote: 'rents' is marginally defensible (some companies charge internal departments); 'borrowers' settles it, but 'loans' as the answer with 'lends' removed, or replacing 'rents' with 'returns', would close the door completely.

v-synonym-04.reason: 'comprise' is transitive: 'the committee comprises five managers'. 'consists' needs 'of'; 'conforms' needs 'to'; 'constitutes' is reversed (the managers constitute the committee).
v-synonym-04.why: consist/comprise/constitute with the 'of' trap is a genuine ETS lexical item.

v-synonym-07.reason: Only 'abide' takes 'by': 'abide by the rules'. 'comply with', 'adhere to', 'conform to' all need different prepositions.
v-synonym-07.why: Four near-synonyms distinguished solely by preposition; this is exactly the harder end of Part 5 vocabulary.

v-synonym-08.reason: Production stops temporarily and 'will resume', so 'suspend'. 'terminate'/'abandon' are permanent; 'conclude' means to finish, contradicting 'resume'.
v-synonym-08.why: 'resume' later in the stem is the disambiguating clue, as in real items; solid.

v-synonym-09.reason: 'waive a fee' is the collocation. 'exempt' takes a person ('exempt guests from the fee'); 'spare'/'relieve' also take the person as object.
v-synonym-09.why: 'exempt' is a strong near-miss (right meaning, wrong syntax); very ETS-like.

v-business-07.reason: An initial 15 percent paid at signing with 'the balance due upon delivery' is a 'deposit'. 'dividend', 'rebate' and 'premium' are unrelated to a partial upfront payment.
v-business-07.why: 'the balance due upon delivery' gives the answer away and the distractors are not close; below typical ETS resistance.
v-business-07.fix: Replace one distractor with 'down payment'-adjacent trap such as 'installment' (plausible but wrong here) and trim the 'balance due' clue.
v-business-07.editorNote: A logistics company receiving a share of a 'purchase price' is a little odd; a supplier or contractor would read more naturally.

v-business-08.reason: 'reconcile bank statements with the ledger' is the accounting collocation, reinforced by 'discrepancies'. 'consolidate' (merge accounts), 'liquidate', 'appraise' do not fit.
v-business-08.why: Domain-specific verb with reasonable distractors; standard TOEIC finance register.

v-family-01.reason: 'keep [details] confidential' (adjective meaning secret). 'confident' is the classic word-family lure but means self-assured; 'confiding'/'confided' are verb forms.
v-family-01.why: confident/confidential is very well known; the stem practically defines the word.
v-family-01.fix: Consider a rarer family (e.g. 'considerable/considerate', 'economic/economical') to raise it to medium.

v-family-07.reason: 'attentive to guests' needs' is the adjective for careful, responsive service. 'attendant' as adjective means accompanying; 'attended'/'attending' do not take 'to ... needs' in this sense.
v-family-07.why: Word-family item with a proper near-miss ('attendant'); fine.

v-family-08.reason: 'complimentary copy' = free; 'complementary' means completing/matching and is the classic homophone lure. 'complimented'/'completed' are wrong forms.
v-family-08.why: complimentary/complementary is a well-known ETS-style pair and the stem gives no unfair clue beyond 'receive ... copy'.

l-qr-03.reason: Alternative question (train or driving). A answers indirectly: parking is expensive, so the speaker is taking the train. B answers 'when', C is a sound trap on 'train/trained'.
l-qr-03.why: Indirect answer to an alternative question with one sound trap and one wrong-wh trap; exactly current Part 2 style.

l-qr-09.reason: 'Who will lead the training?' - B says the decision has not been made yet (it is on Monday's agenda). A names Ms. Harlan, who the question says has retired; C comments on last year's training.
l-qr-09.why: 'Not decided yet' replies are a Part 2 staple; A is a good repeated-name lure.

l-qr-10.reason: C replies with a question implying the reason was already communicated by e-mail, a common indirect answer to 'why'. A begins with 'Because' but answers the wrong question; B answers 'how long', not 'why'.
l-qr-10.why: 'Because' lure plus a wrong-wh answer plus a counter-question: standard ETS Part 2 design.

l-qr-11.reason: A statement that figures 'don't add up' is answered by C, which suggests a possible missing item (April returns). A gives an unrelated statistic; B ('Good, then we can send them') would follow a positive statement, not a problem.
l-qr-11.why: Statement-response item with a counter-question; B is a nice pragmatic trap for candidates who miss 'don't'.

l-qr-12.reason: Request to train the new designer; A implies training is unnecessary because she already knows the system. B is a sound trap on 'booking', C on 'designer/design'.
l-qr-12.why: Indirect refusal/'not needed' reply with two sound traps; this is the harder Part 2 type.

l-conv-05:0.reason: W1: the buyers 'mainly want to see our new packaging line in action' = watch new equipment operate. Painters and maintenance are mentioned as obstacles, not as the visitors' aim.
l-conv-05:0.why: Straightforward purpose question with paraphrase ('line in action' -> 'equipment operate').

l-conv-05:1.reason: W2: on Friday 'the painters have the whole production floor booked, and visitors aren't allowed in while they're working' = part of the facility closed to visitors. A applies to Monday/Tuesday; B and D are not stated.
l-conv-05:1.why: Requires matching the right reason to the right day, with the maintenance reason as a strong lure; good three-speaker design.

l-conv-05:2.reason: Hannah (W2) is asked to order safety gear and says 'I'll call them [the supplier] as soon as we're done here' = contact a vendor. A is what W1 will do; C and D are not mentioned.
l-conv-05:2.why: 'Next action' question that depends on tracking which woman is Hannah; fair.
l-conv-05:2.editorNote: Real ETS three-speaker items usually ask 'What will Hannah do next?' or 'What does Hannah agree to do?' with the name, as here; fine.

l-conv-06:0.reason: M: 'my manager asked me to go to the one right after it' = his supervisor wants him at a different session. The badge (A) is a separate issue; he has heard the speaker is excellent, not poor (C); no client (D).
l-conv-06:0.why: Direct paraphrase (manager -> supervisor) with the badge as a plausible lure.

l-conv-06:1.reason: The contracts workshop is at 1:00 in Room 115; the man will attend 'the one right after it', i.e. 2:30 Leading Remote Teams, Room 310 (also matched by 'work-from-home policy').
l-conv-06:1.why: Correct graphic design: the transcript never says the room or the workshop name, so the candidate must use both the table and 'right after it'. Room 115 is the natural trap.

l-conv-06:2.reason: M: 'I'll head up there and get it now' refers to his badge at the relocated registration desk = pick up his conference pass. The desk is no longer in the main lobby (A); coffee is later (C).
l-conv-06:2.why: Requires resolving 'it' to the badge and ignoring the coffee plan; a fair next-action item.

l-talk-01:0.reason: The announcement is about a contractor 'replacing those elevators' for two weeks and the temporary arrangements = installation of new elevators. No new entrance, hours change or drill is mentioned.
l-talk-01:0.why: Main-idea question; 'replacing' -> 'installation of new' is a mild paraphrase.

l-talk-01:1.reason: 'Those elevators will be very busy between 8:30 and 9:00, so if you can, try to come in a little earlier' = the remaining elevators will be crowded. Nothing about closing early or restricted pass times.
l-talk-01:1.why: Reason question with explicit causal 'so'; the paraphrase 'busy' -> 'crowded' is fair.

l-talk-01:2.reason: 'the front desk can give you a pass for the freight elevator at the back' = access to a service elevator. The maps (A) are posted beside staircases, not given out at the desk.
l-talk-01:2.why: Good detail question: the map option is a real lure because both maps and passes are mentioned in consecutive sentences.

l-talk-03:0.reason: 'our store', 'you'll be off the sales floor all day', 'I'll make sure the store stays covered' identify the listeners as store employees.
l-talk-03:0.why: Inference-of-audience question with clear cues; standard opener.

l-talk-03:1.reason: She has just said each session lasts six hours; 'That's not a typo' means the length is correct and intentional, i.e. the sessions really will last that long.
l-talk-03:1.why: Speaker-intention question with the quoted phrase placed exactly as in real Part 4; A is a well-chosen surface-level lure.

l-talk-03:2.reason: 'Please sign up for one [session] on the sheet by the break room door by Friday' = choose a session date. Training itself must be completed before the end of the month, not by Friday (A).
l-talk-03:2.why: Detail question with a deadline-confusion lure; fair.

overall: Yes, this batch is clearly harder and closer to real ETS items than a typical easy practice set: the stems are long and business-flavoured, the grammar section now carries genuine traps (who/whom with a parenthetical, mandative subjunctive, 'contribute to + -ing', 'Each of ... is', 'Those who ... are', reduced passive relatives), the vocabulary section uses preposition-based near-synonyms and syntactic near-misses ('exempt', 'consists', 'ran short'), and the listening items use indirect Part 2 replies, a properly constructed graphic question and a speaker-intention question. I found no wrong or truly ambiguous keys; every item has a single defensible answer under standard American formal usage. What is still off: about a quarter of the grammar items and several vocab items remain easy (short stems, obvious cues such as 'Currently', 'the balance due', the 'on behalf of' letter formula, 'decided to'), so the set is bottom-heavy compared with a real form; two multi-word-preposition items share 'on behalf of'; and a few stems have small logic or register wrinkles (6 p.m. vs 5 p.m., 'university', repeated 'front desk').
shouldFix: g-prep-05: 'on behalf of' is a distractor here and the key in g-prep-07; replace it (e.g. 'in exchange for').
g-connect-06: 'staffed only until 5 p.m.' vs 'deliveries after 6 p.m.' — align the times or reframe with 'will not accept ... unless'.
g-mandative-03: keep D, but note British formal usage accepts the indicative 'checks'; if you want zero dispute, swap A for 'to check' or 'checking'.
g-tense-02, g-participle-01, g-toing-01, g-prep-07, v-business-07, v-family-01: too easy for the stated goal — lengthen stems, remove giveaway cues or use closer distractors.
v-synonym-02: 'rents' is marginally defensible; 'borrowers' saves it, but a cleaner distractor (e.g. 'returns') would remove the argument.
g-tense-06: 'straight out of university' → 'college' for ETS American register.
'front desk' appears in g-pos-06, g-pos-07, v-family-07 and l-talk-01; vary the setting.
